content.title: About
content.content: Bean cake is a baked product made from ground legumes (usually beans or peas), whole‑grain flour, eggs, vegetable oil and a modest amount of sugar. The cake has a dense yet tender crumb, a subtle nutty flavor and a faint aroma of the beans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bean cake is popular in Asian and South American cuisines as a source of plant protein.
Baking legumes into a batter increases the bioavailability of their nutrients.
Legume‑based cake is more filling than traditional wheat‑flour cakes.
It is often used in vegetarian and vegan diets as a meat‑free snack.
When stored properly, the cake stays fresh for up to a week.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Legumes provide all essential amino acids, making the cake a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes long‑lasting satiety.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Bean cake raises blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals aid energy metabolism and muscle function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytochemicals in legumes help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, peas or soy.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Legumes contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in excess.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions may cause gas and bloating in sensitive people.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the cake is prepared with added salt, intake should be monitored, especially for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bean cake can be enjoyed as a snack on its own, sliced and served with vegetable dips, added to salads, or used in sandwiches. It also reheats well in a microwave or toaster.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cake in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Discard if any mold or off‑smell appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese dip with chili pepper is a smooth spread made from processed cheese, cream and hot chili peppers. It has a creamy texture, a mild heat and a rich cheesy flavor, perfect for snacks, vegetables and chips.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese‑and‑chili combination has been popular in Mexican cuisine for over a century.
Chili peppers contain capsaicin, which gives the heat and may boost metabolism.
The dip is often served as a sauce for nachos because its creamy consistency holds crunchy pieces well.
Many variations exist, adding tomatoes, corn or spices such as cumin and paprika.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cheese base provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Cheese supplies high‑quality protein that supports muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamins B2 and B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties of chili
items.content: Capsaicin and carotenoids in chili have antioxidant effects that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: May aid digestion
items.content: A gentle heat can stimulate gastric secretions, helping digestion.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The dip may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: Very hot versions can irritate the gastrointestinal tract, especially for those with a sensitive stomach.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because of cream and cheese, the dip is calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Prepared versions often contain added salt, which may be a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chilled as a sauce for nachos, chips, vegetable sticks, crackers, or use as a spread in sandwiches and burgers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 5‑7 days. For longer storage, freeze in small portions; thaw and stir before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken grilled and coated with sauce is a popular dish in many cuisines worldwide. The meat is high in protein, and the lack of skin reduces fat content, making it a lighter option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken is one of the most consumed meats globally.
Grilling creates a distinctive flavor through the Maillard reaction.
Various sauces (barbecue, teriyaki, garlic) dramatically change the taste profile.
Chicken provides all essential amino acids.
In some cultures, skinless chicken is considered a healthier choice.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving delivers about 31 g of high‑quality protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Removing the skin cuts saturated fat, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6, and B12, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones, immunity, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Chicken protein is quickly absorbed, making it suitable for athletes and recovery periods.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauces often contain high salt levels; choose low‑sodium versions if you have hypertension.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Some ready‑made sauces may contain artificial preservatives and sweeteners.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless grilled chicken can be served as a main dish, sliced into salads, used in sandwiches, or added to pasta. Sauces can be served on the side or drizzled over the meat just before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions at –18 °C; thaw in the refrigerator before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Chili with meat is a spicy dish made from ground meat (beef, pork or a blend), tomatoes, beans, spices and chili peppers. It is popular in Mexican and American cuisines and is often served with rice, tortillas or bread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally chili is cooked in earthenware pots, allowing flavors to develop slowly.
There are more than 150 varieties of chili peppers, each giving a different level of heat.
The United States hosts the annual World Chili Championship where chefs from many states compete.
In Texas, “chili con carne” is often prepared without beans, while most other regions include them.
Chili with meat is a common comfort food after sporting events.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef and pork contain heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from tomatoes and spices
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and capsaicin from chili have anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Fiber from beans
items.content: Beans add dietary fiber, promoting digestive health.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: Very hot versions can irritate the stomach and esophagus in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared spice mixes often contain a lot of salt; monitor the amount used.

items.title: Allergy to meat or beans
items.content: Some people may be allergic to beef, pork or legumes.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish can be calorie‑rich due to meat and oil; portion control is advised for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve hot chili with meat alongside rice, mashed potatoes, tortillas, croutons or grated cheese. Garnish with sour cream, avocado or fresh herbs as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the chili to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Cookie, marshmallow pie, chocolate covered is a soft cookie with a layer of airy marshmallow in the center, all coated in a thick chocolate glaze. The dessert combines a crunchy cookie texture, sweet fluffy marshmallow, and the bittersweet taste of chocolate.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recipes for this type of cookie appeared in the United States in the 1970s as part of the "soft" dessert trend.
Traditional marshmallow was originally made from the root of the marshmallow plant, but today gelatin or plant‑based alternatives are used.
Chocolate glaze is often a blend of dark and milk chocolate to balance flavor.
Cookies can be round or shaped as mini bars, making them convenient for snacking.
The contrast of textures makes the product popular with both children and adults seeking a multi‑sensory treat.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Chocolate, especially dark chocolate, contains flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from the cookie and marshmallow raise blood sugar rapidly, providing an instant energy lift.

items.title: Contains a modest amount of protein
items.content: Recipes often use egg whites, adding a small amount of protein.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin production, which can improve mood.

items.title: Calcium from dairy ingredients
items.content: Milk chocolate and occasional milk added to the dough supply calcium.

items.title: Gluten and dairy allergies
items.content: The cookie typically contains wheat flour and dairy, which may trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Marshmallow and chocolate make the product very sweet, contributing to tooth decay and blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Due to sugars, fats, and carbs, a serving can be calorie‑rich, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Some commercial versions use partially hydrogenated oils that contain trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a standalone treat, crumble it over ice cream, use it to garnish cakes, or simply snack on it between meals. Slightly warming it can melt the chocolate glaze and soften the marshmallow for an extra indulgent experience.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place at 59‑72 °F (15‑22 °C). For longer shelf life (over two weeks) keep refrigerated to prevent the chocolate from melting. Avoid direct sunlight, which can cause the glaze to discolor.

content.title: About
content.content: The chocolate ice cream cone is a ready‑to‑eat dessert consisting of a crisp waffle cone coated with a thin layer of chocolate and filled with a portion of ice cream. It is individually wrapped, which preserves flavor and texture for extended storage.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first ice cream cone appeared in the early 1920s in the United States.
The chocolate coating often contains small pieces of nuts or caramel for extra flavor.
Aluminum foil packaging protects the product from light and moisture, extending shelf life up to 6 months.
In some markets the cones are sold in “mini” sizes to help control portion size.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Ice cream made from dairy provides calcium, essential for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Dairy products contain vitamins B2 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Small amount of protein
items.content: The ice cream contributes a modest amount of protein useful for tissue repair.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The product contains milk and may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to lactose or casein.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Both the chocolate coating and the ice cream contain significant sugar, which can contribute to weight gain if consumed frequently.

items.title: Temperature sensitivity
items.content: Storing above +4 °C can cause the ice cream to melt and the chocolate layer to become sticky.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Remove the cone from its wrapper, let it sit at room temperature for 2–3 minutes so the chocolate softens slightly, and enjoy immediately. Do not cut the cone, as this may cause the ice cream to spill.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C or lower. Once removed from the wrapper, consume within 30 minutes to avoid melting. Do not store at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Kidney beans are large, meaty, red‑colored beans widely used in many cuisines. They are rich in protein, fiber, complex carbohydrates, and a range of vitamins and minerals. Beans are typically boiled, stewed, or added to salads, soups, and chili.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the bean’s shape, which resembles a kidney.
Several varieties exist: red, light‑red and dark‑red, each with its own flavor and texture.
Raw beans contain phytohemagglutinin – a toxin that is destroyed only by prolonged boiling (at least 10 minutes).
Kidney beans are a staple in South American, Mexican, and Caribbean dishes.
In the United States kidney beans are listed among foods that support heart health.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked beans provides about 15 g of protein, making it an excellent protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are essential for blood formation and anemia prevention, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for diabetes management and weight control.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in beans help combat free radicals.

items.title: Toxins in raw beans
items.content: Raw or undercooked beans can cause food poisoning. Always boil them for at least 10 minutes.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: High levels of oligosaccharides may cause flatulence; soaking and rinsing reduce this effect.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may develop an allergic reaction to legumes.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Beans contain vitamin K, which can affect the efficacy of anticoagulant drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add kidney beans to chili, soups, stews, salads, and side dishes. Before cooking, soak them for 6–8 hours, rinse well, then boil. Cooked beans store well in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or can be frozen for longer keeping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place – up to 1 year. Cooked beans should be kept in a sealed container in the fridge for no more than 5 days, or frozen for extended storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Lamb or mutton is the meat of sheep, often served with a savory gravy made from broth, tomatoes and spices. Tender, juicy and slightly sweet, it is rich in protein and iron. Traditionally the dish is slow‑cooked so the meat becomes melt‑in‑your‑mouth and absorbs the sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb is one of the oldest meats consumed by humans.
Different cuisines have their own gravy styles: Indian curry, Mediterranean tomato‑olive sauce, or French red wine reduction.
Lamb is a staple of festive meals, such as Easter pilaf or Scottish haggis.
The meat is high in creatine, which supports muscle energy.
Traditionally lamb is cooked over open fire or in earthenware pots, giving it a distinctive flavor.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Lamb provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High in iron
items.content: Heme iron from lamb is easily absorbed, helping prevent anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12, niacin and riboflavin, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals boost immune health and protect against oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Lamb contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lamb proteins.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor bacteria such as Salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Lamb is rich in purines, which can be problematic for people with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve lamb with gravy over mashed potatoes, rice, couscous or fresh vegetables. Typically the meat is cut into chunks and simmered in the gravy for 2–3 hours until tender. It also works well baked in the oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh lamb in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen lamb can be stored at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or a gray color; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato French Fries with Chili are deep‑fried potato sticks tossed in a spicy sauce made from chili peppers, spices, and sometimes tomato paste. The dish is a staple of fast‑food restaurants and street vendors, offering a crunchy, hot snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: French fries originated in the United States in the early 20th century and quickly became an iconic fast‑food item.
The chili sauce often uses jalapeño, serrano, or cayenne peppers, giving the dish varying levels of heat.
In some countries the fries are served with cheese sauce, but the classic chili version relies solely on the spicy topping.
Traditionally the potatoes are cut into 0.5–1 cm sticks to achieve a crisp exterior and a soft interior.
The dish is commonly served in cardboard containers, making it easy to eat on the go.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins source
items.content: Potatoes contain vitamin B6 and B3, important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Antioxidants in chili
items.content: Capsaicin and other compounds in chili have antioxidant properties that help protect cells.

items.title: Metabolism boost
items.content: Spicy foods can temporarily increase thermogenesis, aiding calorie burning.

items.title: Improved digestion
items.content: Spices in the sauce may stimulate gastric juice production, supporting digestion.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Deep‑fried potatoes and oily sauce make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Spiciness of chili
items.content: Very hot peppers can cause heartburn or stomach irritation in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may be allergic to potatoes or ingredients in the sauce.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Salt added during frying and in the sauce raises sodium intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fries hot, typically in a paper container or on a plate. Eat with fingers, a fork, or dip them in additional sauce. For a lighter option, choose baked fries and a milder chili sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared fries are best consumed within 2–3 hours at room temperature. For longer storage, cool them to room temperature, then place in an airtight container in the refrigerator (up to 24 hours). Reheat in an oven to restore crispness.

split-peas-from-dried-no-added-fat.title: Split peas, dried, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Split peas are dried pea seeds that have been cut in half. They contain no added fat and are a rich source of plant protein, complex carbohydrates, and dietary fiber. Split peas are commonly used in soups, purees, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Split peas cook faster than whole peas because of their halved shape.
They are a staple in many cuisines, such as Indian dal, British pea soup, and Russian shchi.
Dried split peas have a long shelf life when stored in a cool, dry place.
Peas are high in iron, making them useful for preventing anemia.
Compared with whole peas, split peas produce a smoother texture when cooked.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: One cup of cooked split peas provides about 16 g of protein, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates give sustained energy and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B6, and folate are involved in metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Minerals: iron, magnesium, phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation, bone health, and muscle function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Anti‑nutrient content
items.content: Raw peas contain phytic acid and lectins that can reduce mineral absorption; they should be fully cooked.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: High fiber content may cause bloating or flatulence in sensitive people.

items.title: Not suitable for certain kidney conditions
items.content: The relatively high purine content can increase kidney load in people with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook split peas for 20‑30 minutes until tender, then use them in soups, purees, salads, or as a side. They can be added to vegetable stews or processed into a vegetarian mince.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried split peas in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored, they keep for 2‑3 years.
